sections.heading: The early dynasties of Andhra — the foundations

blocks.text: Ancient Andhra's political history opens with the **Satavahanas (c. 2nd cent. BCE – 3rd cent. CE)** — the first great Deccan empire — followed by the **Ikshvakus, Salankayanas, Pallavas (early phase) and Vishnukundins**. Together they made the **Krishna-Godavari deltas** a hub of **trade, Buddhism, Sanskrit-Prakrit-Telugu culture and monumental art (Amaravati)** — the bedrock on which later Andhra civilisation was built.

rows: **Satavahanas**
c. 2nd BCE–3rd CE; capital **Pratishthana (Paithan) / Dhanyakataka**; **Gautamiputra Satakarni** the greatest; **Hala** (Gathasaptashati); Roman trade, Amaravati Buddhism, first Deccan empire.
**Ikshvakus**
3rd–4th CE; capital **Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda)**; great **Buddhist** patrons (esp. royal women); Nagarjunakonda stupas & university.
**Salankayanas**
4th–5th CE; capital **Vengi**; feudatories-turned-independent; Vengi becomes a lasting political centre.
**Pallavas (early)** & **Vishnukundins**
Early Pallavas held parts of coastal Andhra; **Vishnukundins (5th–6th CE)** — capital Vengi/Denduluru; **Madhavavarman** greatest; bridge to the Eastern Chalukyas.

sections.heading: The Satavahana keystone

items: **Political**: the Satavahanas unified the Deccan after the Mauryas, resisting the **Western Kshatrapas (Sakas)**; **Gautamiputra Satakarni** (Nasik prashasti of his mother **Gautami Balasri**) is celebrated as the destroyer of the Sakas and restorer of Brahmanical order.
**Economy & trade**: a flourishing **Indo-Roman maritime trade** (ports, Roman coins), guilds (shrenis), and a monetised economy; the deltas were the granary and the coast the emporium.

**Religion & society**: **Brahmanism revived (Vedic sacrifices) alongside strong Buddhist patronage** — the great stupa at **Amaravati** and the caves of the western Deccan; a notable role for **royal women** and the matronymic naming (Gautamiputra, Vasishthiputra).
**Culture**: **Prakrit** the court language (Hala's Gathasaptashati), early Telugu presence, and the beginnings of the distinctive **Amaravati school of art** (HCOA-046).

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — Andhra's early dynasties

items: **The foundation layer:** the **Andhras** are mentioned in the Aitareya Brahmana and by Megasthenes (a powerful people with 30 walled towns); early ruling houses — **Mauryan overlordship → Satavahanas → Ikshvakus → Vishnukundins**.
**Ikshvakus (Nagarjunakonda/Vijayapuri):** succeeded the Satavahanas in the Krishna valley; great patrons of Buddhism (the Mahachaitya), with notable women donors (queens).
**Vishnukundins:** a major post-Ikshvaku Deccan power that promoted Brahmanism and Telugu-region culture, bridging to the Eastern Chalukyas.
**Significance:** Andhra was a continuously important political and Buddhist-cultural region from the earliest historical period.

sections.heading: Social, economic & religious life; language in ancient Andhra

blocks.text: Under the early Andhra dynasties (Satavahana–Vishnukundin) emerged a **prosperous, trade-based, religiously plural society** in which **Brahmanism and Buddhism flourished together**, guilds organised production, and the **Telugu language began its documented journey** amid a Prakrit-Sanskrit court culture — the social bedrock of Andhra civilisation.

rows: **Society**
**Varna order with regional flexibility**; prominent **guilds (shrenis)** of artisans/merchants; notable **status of women** (matronymics, women donors at stupas); a cosmopolitan coast.
**Economy**
**Agrarian delta base + brisk trade** (Roman, Southeast Asian); ports, coinage, craft guilds; irrigation tanks; a monetised, urbanising economy.
**Religion**
**Brahmanism** (Vedic sacrifices — the Satavahanas performed asvamedha) coexisting with **vigorous Buddhism** (Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda) and early **Jainism**; genuine pluralism.
**Language**
**Prakrit** the early court/inscriptional language, **Sanskrit** rising (Vishnukundins), and the **earliest traces of Telugu** in place-names and words within inscriptions.

sections.heading: The rise of Telugu and religious balance

items: **Religious balance (the key theme)**: royal patronage was **plural** — the same dynasties endowed Vedic sacrifices AND Buddhist stupas; present this as **coexistence**, the hallmark of ancient-Andhra religious life, not competition.

**Buddhism's Andhra golden age**: **Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Ghantasala, Bhattiprolu** made coastal Andhra a **Buddhist heartland**; the philosopher **Nagarjuna (Madhyamaka/Sunyavada)** is associated with Nagarjunakonda — Andhra's greatest gift to Buddhist thought.

**Economic sinews**: **guilds** regulated crafts and even acted as bankers; **Indo-Roman and Southeast-Asian trade** (Andhra merchants reached Suvarnabhumi) underwrote the donative Buddhism carved in stone.

**Language journey**: from **Prakrit inscriptions** (Satavahana) to **Sanskrit** (Vishnukundin charters), with **Telugu words/place-names surfacing** — the documented pre-history of Telugu that flowers later (HCOA-050).

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — Satavahana society & the rise of Telugu

items: **Society & economy:** a prosperous agrarian-cum-trading society; **Indo-Roman maritime trade** (Amaravati, Kodavali; Roman coins), guilds, and coastal ports; Prakrit as court language with early Telugu words appearing.
**Religious balance:** Satavahanas patronised **both Brahmanism (Vedic sacrifices — Gautamiputra) and Buddhism (Amaravati stupa)** — a model of religious pluralism.
**Language:** the Satavahana period is the seedbed from which **Telugu** later emerged as a literary language (fully flowering under the Eastern Chalukyas).
**Significance:** Andhra under the Satavahanas was a cosmopolitan hub linking the Deccan interior to Indian Ocean trade.

sections.heading: Literature, art & architecture; Jainism & Buddhism in Andhra

blocks.text: Ancient Andhra produced a **distinctive artistic-religious civilisation** — the **Amaravati school of sculpture**, the great **Buddhist stupas and monastic universities** of the Krishna valley, early **Prakrit literature (Hala)**, and a strong presence of **Jainism** — making the region one of **India's foremost early centres of Buddhist art and thought**.

rows: **Art — Amaravati school**

A distinct sculptural style (2nd BCE–3rd CE) — **white-marble (Palnad limestone) reliefs, narrative panels, graceful slender figures, crowded compositions**; influenced Southeast-Asian & Sri Lankan art.
**Architecture — stupas**
**Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu, Ghantasala** — great **stupas, chaityas, viharas** and a monastic **university at Nagarjunakonda**.
**Literature**
**Hala's Gathasaptashati** (Prakrit lyric anthology); **Gunadhya's Brihatkatha** (in Paisachi, tradition); a rich Prakrit-Sanskrit base preceding Telugu literature.
**Jainism & Buddhism**
**Buddhism** dominant on the coast (Hinayana → Mahayana; Nagarjuna); **Jainism** present (Bhattiprolu, later Kadamba-Ganga links) — a plural religious landscape.

sections.heading: The Amaravati legacy and religious currents

items: **The Amaravati school (the signature)**: one of **India's three great early art schools** (with Gandhara & Mathura) — but purely **Indian in idiom**, marked by dynamic narrative reliefs and slender, sinuous figures; the **Amaravati Mahastupa** was its masterpiece; its influence travelled to **Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia**.

**Buddhism's evolution in Andhra**: from **Hinayana to Mahayana**, with Andhra a cradle of **Mahayana thought (Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka)** and later Vajrayana currents; the coast was studded with monasteries sustained by trade wealth.

**Jainism's presence**: attested at **Bhattiprolu** and in later Andhra (Rashtrakuta/Ganga contacts, Kadambas); it contributed to early literature and left cave/relic sites, part of the plural fabric.

**Literary bedrock**: **Prakrit (Hala) and Sanskrit** literature under the early dynasties laid the linguistic-cultural ground from which **Telugu literature would later rise (HCOA-050)** — continuity across the ancient-medieval divide.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the Amaravati school of art

items: **The Amaravati school:** one of the **three great ancient Indian art schools** (with Gandhara & Mathura) — white-marble (Palnad limestone) relief sculpture, narrative Jataka panels, and the 'lotus-medallion' style, deeply influential across Southeast Asia.
**Buddhist centres:** **Amaravati, Nagarjunakonda, Bhattiprolu (early relic casket with Brahmi), Ghantasala, Salihundam** — a dense stupa landscape.
**Jainism:** also present in early Andhra (e.g., sites in Rayalaseema) before Hindu revival.
**Significance:** Andhra was a fountainhead of Buddhist art whose influence radiated to Sri Lanka and Southeast Asia — a strong civilisational-pride point.

sections.heading: The later dynasties — Eastern Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Renati Cholas

blocks.text: The early-medieval centuries (**7th–12th CE**) saw Andhra shaped by the **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** — the longest-ruling and most consequential dynasty — in interplay with the **Rashtrakutas** of the western Deccan and the **Renati Cholas** of Rayalaseema. This era **consolidated Telugu identity**: the first Telugu inscriptions, the first Telugu literary work, and a synthesis of Deccan cultures that defined medieval Andhra.

rows: **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi**

c. 624–1075 CE; founded by **Kubja Vishnuvardhana** (brother of Pulakeshin II); ruled coastal Andhra ~400 yrs from **Vengi**; patronised **Telugu** — **Nannaya** (Adikavi) under **Rajaraja Narendra**; merged with the Cholas.
**Rashtrakutas**

8th–10th CE; western-Deccan imperial power (**Manyakheta**); overlords/rivals of the Eastern Chalukyas; great patrons of art (**Ellora Kailasa**) and Kannada/Sanskrit-Jain culture, influencing Andhra.
**Renati Cholas**
Ruled **Renadu (Rayalaseema — Cuddapah region)**; significant for the **earliest Telugu inscriptions (Erragudipadu / Kalamalla, ~575 CE)** — a landmark for the Telugu language.
**Others**
**Telugu Cholas, Vaidumbas, Banas** — minor Rayalaseema/border dynasties feeding the same cultural stream.

sections.heading: Socio-cultural life and the making of Telugu identity

items: **The Eastern Chalukya keystone**: their **four-century Vengi rule** gave coastal Andhra political continuity and, crucially, **royal patronage to Telugu** — the reign of **Rajaraja Narendra** saw **Nannaya** begin the **Telugu Mahabharatam**, the fountainhead of Telugu literature (HCOA-050).

**The earliest Telugu (the milestone)**: the **Renati Chola inscriptions of Rayalaseema (Kalamalla, c. 575 CE)** are among the **first Telugu-language inscriptions** — evidence that Telugu had become a written language of administration in the border regions.

**Deccan synthesis**: the tussle between the **Rashtrakutas (west) and Eastern Chalukyas (east)** made Andhra a meeting ground of **Kannada, Sanskrit, Jain and Telugu** currents; society was agrarian-feudal (nayaka/samanta chiefs), religiously plural (Shaivism, Vaishnavism, Jainism, declining Buddhism).

**Religion's shift**: **Buddhism declined** and **Brahmanical Hinduism (Shaiva-Vaishnava) with temple-centred society rose**, alongside strong **Jainism** under Rashtrakuta influence — the temple economy that Kakatiya/Reddi Andhra would inherit.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — the Eastern Chalukyas & Telugu's literary dawn

items: **Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi:** ruled coastal Andhra for ~500 years; under their patronage **Nannaya** (11th c., court of Rajaraja Narendra) began the Telugu **Mahabharata** — the 'Adi Kavi' and the dawn of Telugu literature.
**Cultural synthesis:** a balance of Vedic Brahmanism, Jainism and Shaivism; temple-building and Sanskrit-Telugu bilingual culture.
**Political context:** the Vengi throne was the prize in the long **Chola-Chalukya wars**, keeping Andhra central to Deccan geopolitics.
**Significance:** the Eastern Chalukyas midwifed Telugu as a literary language — the linguistic foundation of Andhra identity.

prelimsPointers: **Nannaya** — 'Adi Kavi' (first poet); began the Telugu Mahabharata under Eastern Chalukya Rajaraja Narendra.
**Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi** — patrons of the Telugu literary dawn.

**Rashtrakutas** — western-Deccan power; capital **Manyakheta**; built **Ellora Kailasa temple**.
**Renati Cholas** — ruled **Renadu (Rayalaseema)**; **Kalamalla/Erragudipadu inscription (~575 CE)** among the earliest Telugu inscriptions.
Minor lines — **Telugu Cholas, Vaidumbas, Banas** in Rayalaseema/border areas.

sections.heading: Telugu script & language; literature, art & architecture (early medieval)

blocks.text: The early-medieval centuries **crystallised the Telugu script and literary tradition**: evolving from the **Brahmi → Kadamba/Chalukya** scripts, Telugu became a full literary language with **Nannaya's Mahabharatam (11th cent.)**, while temple architecture and sculpture flowered under Chalukya-Rashtrakuta-Kakatiya patronage — the artistic idiom that culminates in the Kakatiya masterpieces.

rows: **Script**
**Brahmi → Bhattiprolu/Kadamba → Telugu-Kannada script → distinct Telugu script**; the shared Telugu-Kannada parent split into separate scripts in the early-medieval era.
**Language & literature**
Telugu matured from inscriptional to literary; **Nannaya (11th c.)** — Adikavi — began the **Andhra Mahabharatam** in the **champu** (prose-verse) style, fixing literary Telugu grammar & diction.
**Architecture**
The **Vesara (Deccan) temple style** — a Nagara-Dravida blend under the Chalukyas-Rashtrakutas; leading to **Kakatiya** temples (Thousand-Pillar temple, Ramappa) and their signature toranas.
**Sculpture & fine arts**
Rich temple sculpture, the **Kakatiya kirti-torana (Warangal gateway)**, dance-music traditions (the Nritta Ratnavali), and continued Jain art in Rayalaseema.

sections.heading: The literary dawn and architectural idiom

items: **Nannaya's dawn (the milestone)**: **Nannaya Bhattaraka**, patronised by **Rajaraja Narendra (Eastern Chalukya)**, began the **Telugu Mahabharatam** — earning the title **Adikavi (first poet)** and setting the **champu** template; completed later by **Tikkana & Errapragada** (the **Kavitraya — trinity of poets**).

**Script evolution**: the **Telugu script** descends via **Brahmi and the Telugu-Kannada common script**, separating into its rounded modern form in the early-medieval centuries — inscriptions trace the whole journey.

**The Vesara temple tradition**: Andhra-Deccan temple architecture blended **Nagara (north) and Dravida (south)** into the **Vesara** style — refined by the **Kakatiyas** (Hanamkonda Thousand-Pillar temple, the **Ramappa temple — a UNESCO site**, star-shaped platforms, floating bricks, black-basalt polish).

**Fine arts**: Kakatiya-era **kirti-toranas (Warangal Fort gateways)**, temple sculpture, and treatises like **Jayapa Senani's Nritta Ratnavali** on dance — an integrated art-architecture culture that HCOA-051 develops.

sections.heading: Answer craft

items: Two pillars: the LITERARY dawn (Nannaya/Adikavi → Kavitraya, champu style, script evolution Brahmi→Telugu) and the ARCHITECTURAL idiom (Vesara → Kakatiya Ramappa/Thousand-Pillar temples, kirti-toranas).
Ramappa (UNESCO), floating bricks and the kirti-torana are the memorable, high-value specifics.

blocks.text: Exam tip: Pair the literary dawn (Nannaya the Adikavi, the champu style, Brahmi-to-Telugu script) with the architectural idiom (Vesara → Kakatiya Ramappa & Thousand-Pillar temples, kirti-toranas) — the twin foundations of medieval Telugu high culture.

sections.heading: 🏺 Deep mastery — Telugu script, literature & early architecture

items: **Script:** Telugu script evolved from **Brahmi** via the Bhattiprolu and Telugu-Kannada scripts — one of the classical Indian writing systems; **Telugu has classical-language status (2008)**.
**Literary foundation:** the **Kavitrayam** (Nannaya, Tikkana, Yerrapragada) completed the Telugu Mahabharata over three centuries — the bedrock of the canon.
**Early architecture:** cave and structural temples of the Vishnukundin/Eastern Chalukya era; the emerging Deccan temple idiom that the Kakatiyas and Vijayanagara would elaborate.
**Significance:** the maturation of script + literature + architecture created a distinct Telugu cultural sphere by the medieval period.

prelimsPointers: **Telugu** granted **classical-language status in 2008**.
**Kavitrayam** (Trinity of poets): Nannaya, Tikkana, Yerrapragada — the Telugu Mahabharata.
**Telugu script** evolved: **Brahmi → Bhattiprolu/Kadamba → Telugu-Kannada common script → distinct Telugu script**.
**Nannaya (11th c.)** — **Adikavi**; began the **Andhra Mahabharatam** in **champu** style under **Rajaraja Narendra**.
**Kavitraya (trinity)** — **Nannaya, Tikkana, Errapragada** — completed the Telugu Mahabharatam.
**Vesara style** — a Nagara-Dravida blend of Deccan temple architecture.
**Ramappa (Rudreswara) temple** — Kakatiya, **UNESCO World Heritage**; famed 'floating bricks' & black-basalt sculpture.
**Thousand-Pillar temple (Hanamkonda)** and **Warangal kirti-toranas** — Kakatiya masterpieces.
**Jayapa Senani's Nritta Ratnavali** — a Kakatiya-era treatise on dance.
mainsAngles: Trace the evolution of the Telugu script and the birth of Telugu literature under the Eastern Chalukyas.
Assess Nannaya's contribution as the Adikavi and founder of the champu literary tradition.
Analyse the Vesara style and its culmination in Kakatiya temple architecture.
Discuss the Ramappa temple as a masterpiece of medieval Andhra architecture and engineering.
Examine the integration of literature, architecture and performing arts in early-medieval Andhra.

glossary.definition: The 'first poet' — the title of Nannaya, who began the Telugu Mahabharatam in the 11th century.
A literary style mixing prose (gadya) and verse (padya), used by Nannaya for the Telugu Mahabharatam.
The 'trinity of poets' — Nannaya, Tikkana and Errapragada — who together rendered the Mahabharatam into Telugu.
The Deccan temple style blending northern (Nagara) and southern (Dravida) features, developed under Chalukya-Rashtrakuta-Kakatiya rule.
An ornamental free-standing gateway/arch; the Warangal Fort kirti-toranas are Kakatiya emblems (part of Telangana's state emblem).
